stem:
David is a 2-year-old boy with a history of frequent intermittent asthma. His asthma has been well controlled on fluticasone (Flixotide) 50 micrograms 1 puff twice daily and salbutamol (Ventolin). His mother asks whether an “asthma pill” could be an option for him.

For which type of asthma have leukotriene receptor antagonists (LTRAs) been demonstrated to be effective?

options.text: There is evidence to support the use of LTRAs in children with exercise-induced asthma
There is evidence to support the use of LTRAs in children with intermittent viral-induced asthma
There is evidence to favour the use of LTRAs to replace inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) in moderate to severe asthma

explanation: Leukotriene receptor antagonists such as montelukast have evidence of benefit in some children with exercise-induced asthma, but they are not preferred as replacement therapy for inhaled corticosteroids in moderate to severe asthma. Evidence for routine use in intermittent viral-induced asthma is less consistent.

citations.title: Practice Quiz: Asthma Management: Medications and Devices - Part A

rationale: The best-supported indication among the options is exercise-induced asthma.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. LTRAs can help prevent exercise-induced bronchoconstriction in some children.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect. Evidence is not strong enough to support routine use for intermittent viral-induced asthma.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect. LTRAs are not favoured over inhaled corticosteroids for moderate to severe asthma.
